title: Classic and Asian forms of massage
intro: Massage is a hands-on treatment in which a therapist presses, rubs and moves the soft tissues of the body. People use it for relaxation, muscle tension and pain. Classic Western massage and Asian forms such as shiatsu and Thai massage differ in technique, but evidence suggests the benefits are mostly short term.

sections.heading: Classic massage
paragraphs: Classic or Swedish massage uses stroking, kneading, pressure and tapping on muscles, usually with oil. It aims to relax muscles, improve blood flow and ease pain and stress. It is often applied to the back, neck and shoulders. Therapists adjust pressure to your needs.

sections.heading: Asian forms
paragraphs: Shiatsu from Japan uses finger, thumb and palm pressure on points along the body, often on a mat while clothed, together with stretching. Thai massage combines pressure and passive yoga-like stretches. Other forms include acupressure and Tuina from China. These traditions describe energy channels, which have no scientific confirmation, although the physical techniques may relax muscles.

sections.heading: What evidence shows
paragraphs: Massage can reduce muscle tension and provide short-term relief of back and neck pain, and many people feel calmer afterwards. Studies find limited evidence of long-lasting benefit for most conditions. Benefits probably come from relaxation, touch and attention. Massage does not cure illnesses.

sections.heading: Risks and who should be careful
paragraphs: Massage is generally safe. Soreness or bruising can follow strong pressure. Avoid massage over inflamed, infected or injured areas, wounds, recent fractures, areas with blood clots or tumours, and during fever. Tell the therapist about pregnancy, bleeding disorders, blood thinners, osteoporosis, heart conditions or cancer. Deep neck manipulation carries rare risks.

sections.heading: Choosing a therapist
paragraphs: Look for a trained, qualified therapist, clear information on cost and what to expect. Insurance may cover massage prescribed by a doctor for specific conditions, but not wellness massage. Speak up if pressure is too strong or you feel pain. A massage should never replace medical assessment of ongoing symptoms.

examples.title: Trying massage for neck tension
examples.text: Imagine you have tight shoulders after desk work. You could book a classic massage, tell the therapist about the neck, and combine it with stretching and breaks.

examples.title: Telling the therapist
examples.text: Suppose you take blood thinners. You might mention this beforehand so that the therapist adjusts pressure.
